candidate: This paper presents a study evaluating the use of nanopore sequencing combined with adaptive sampling and a novel tool called NanoExpansion to accurately characterize repeat expansion disorders. The objective was to improve the diagnostic accuracy and efficiency of identifying these disorders, which are caused by abnormal expansions of short tandem repeats (STRs). The study included 132 participants, including patients with myotonic dystrophy type 1 (DM1), DM2, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), and other neurodegenerative conditions, as well as healthy controls. Native DNA was sequenced using adaptive sampling on Oxford Nanopore platforms, and NanoExpansion was developed to analyze the data, identifying expanded alleles and detecting sequence interruptions. The results showed that nanopore sequencing with NanoExpansion accurately characterized all cases of DM1, DM2, ALS, Friedreich ataxia, Huntington’s disease, and Kennedy disease, and identified several cases of spinocerebellar ataxias (SCAs) and cerebellar ataxia with neuropathy and vestibular areflexia syndrome (CANVAS). Compared to long PCR, nanopore sequencing provided more accurate results for larger expansions, and detected repeat interruptions in a significant proportion of DM1 cases. However, the study noted limitations, including the potential for sequencing errors and the need for further validation on larger datasets. The findings suggest that the integration of nanopore sequencing and NanoExpansion offers a promising approach for the comprehensive characterization of repeat expansion disorders, with the potential to improve routine genetic diagnosis.

Abstract
Expansion repeat disorders are caused by abnormal expansions of short tandem repeats (STRs). We evaluated targeted long-read nanopore
sequencing for comprehensive characterization of STR expansions in 132 participants, including patients with myotonic dystrophy type 1 (DM1,
n = 51) and DM2 ( n = 3) already characterized by Southern blot, C9orf72 -associated amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS n = 11) evaluated by
repeat primed polymerase chain reaction (RP-PCR; validation group), suspected spinocerebellar ataxia (SCA, n = 46), cerebellar ataxia with
neuropathy and vestibular areflexia syndrome (CANVAS; n = 13), Huntington’s disease (1), Kennedy disease (1), Friedreich ataxia (FRDA, 2), and
4 healthy controls (test group). Native DNA was sequenced using adaptive sampling (AS) on Oxford Nanopore GridION or PromethION-2Solo
platforms. Long-PCR sequencing was performed for comparison. We also developed NanoExpansion, a Python-based tool for sizing expanded
alleles and detecting sequence interruptions. We correctly characterized all DM1, DM2, ALS, FRDA, Huntington’s disease, and Kennedy disease
cases, and identified eight SCA27B, two SCA37, three SCA31, one SCA3, and nine CANVAS cases. Compared with the AS approach, long-
PCR underestimated alleles exceeding 800 repeats. Repeat interruptions were detected in 27/51 (52.9%) DM1 cases and 1/10 (10%) ALS, but
not in CANVAS, FRDA, Huntington’s disease, Kennedy disease, or SCA cases. This integrated sequencing analysis pipeline provides accurate,
comprehensive characterization of repeat expansion disorders and has the potential to improve routine genetic diagnosis.

candidate: This study evaluates the diagnostic utility of Oxford Nanopore Technologies (ONT) long-read sequencing, combined with adaptive sampling (AS) and a novel Python-based tool, NanoExpansion, for characterizing repeat expansion disorders (REDs). The researchers analyzed native DNA and long-PCR products from 132 participants, including patients with myotonic dystrophy type 1 (DM1), myotonic dystrophy type 2 (DM2), C9orf72-associated amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), and various spinocerebellar ataxias (SCAs), alongside healthy controls. Results demonstrated that ONT sequencing accurately characterized all DM1, DM2, ALS, Friedreich ataxia, Huntington’s disease, and Kennedy disease cases. Specifically, the pipeline correctly identified expansions in 82% of DM1 subjects, with high correlation between native and long-PCR estimates for smaller expansions (≤800 repeats). The study also identified several SCA and CANVAS cases, though long-PCR showed poor agreement for CANVAS due to high GC content. While the "super-accurate" (sup) basecalling model significantly reduced errors compared to the "high-accuracy" (hac) model, the study was limited by a relatively small cohort size and the need for further multi-center validation. The authors conclude that this integrated pipeline provides a comprehensive, efficient framework for RED diagnosis.

Abstract
Expansion repeat disorders are caused by abnormal expansions of short tandem repeats (STRs). We evaluated targeted long-read nanopore
sequencing for comprehensive characterization of STR expansions in 132 participants, including patients with myotonic dystrophy type 1 (DM1,
n = 51) and DM2 ( n = 3) already characterized by Southern blot, C9orf72 -associated amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS n = 11) evaluated by
repeat primed polymerase chain reaction (RP-PCR; validation group), suspected spinocerebellar ataxia (SCA, n = 46), cerebellar ataxia with
neuropathy and vestibular areflexia syndrome (CANVAS; n = 13), Huntington’s disease (1), Kennedy disease (1), Friedreich ataxia (FRDA, 2), and
4 healthy controls (test group). Native DNA was sequenced using adaptive sampling (AS) on Oxford Nanopore GridION or PromethION-2Solo
platforms. Long-PCR sequencing was performed for comparison. We also developed NanoExpansion, a Python-based tool for sizing expanded
alleles and detecting sequence interruptions. We correctly characterized all DM1, DM2, ALS, FRDA, Huntington’s disease, and Kennedy disease
cases, and identified eight SCA27B, two SCA37, three SCA31, one SCA3, and nine CANVAS cases. Compared with the AS approach, long-
PCR underestimated alleles exceeding 800 repeats. Repeat interruptions were detected in 27/51 (52.9%) DM1 cases and 1/10 (10%) ALS, but
not in CANVAS, FRDA, Huntington’s disease, Kennedy disease, or SCA cases. This integrated sequencing analysis pipeline provides accurate,
comprehensive characterization of repeat expansion disorders and has the potential to improve routine genetic diagnosis.

candidate: This study investigated the role of well-being comparisons in mental health outcomes following loss, using a two-wave longitudinal design with 315 bereaved individuals. The objective was to examine whether aversive well-being comparisons—such as social, temporal, counterfactual, and expectation-based comparisons—predicted higher psychopathology, including prolonged grief disorder (PGD), posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD), depression, anxiety, somatic symptoms, and loneliness. The study also explored whether these comparisons mediated the relationship between comparison frequency and mental health symptoms. Participants completed assessments six months apart, evaluating well-being comparisons, worry, rumination, avoidance, childhood adversity, and mental health outcomes. Preregistered hypotheses were partially supported: higher frequency of aversive well-being comparisons, comparison discrepancy, and negative comparison affective impact predicted elevated psychopathology six months later. These effects remained significant after controlling for autoregressive pathways, worry, rumination, avoidance, and childhood adversity. Mediation analyses suggested that frequent comparisons amplified perceived discrepancies, leading to negative affective impact, which in turn contributed to depression, anxiety, and somatic symptoms. The study found that well-being comparisons played a significant role in mental health outcomes following loss, with aversive comparisons contributing uniquely to psychopathology. However, the study had limitations, including a relatively small sample size and potential underpowering for mediation effects. The findings suggest that interventions targeting maladaptive well-being comparisons may be beneficial for bereaved individuals. The study highlights the importance of understanding cognitive processes like well-being comparisons in the context of grief and mental health.

   Antecedentes: La pérdida de un ser querido puede dar lugar al trastorno de duelo prolongado
   (TDP), al trastorno de estrés postraumático (TEPT), así como a depresión, ansiedad, síntomas
   somáticos y soledad. El pensamiento comparativo sobre el propio bienestar (por ejemplo,
   comparaciones sociales, temporales, contrafácticas o basadas en expectativas) puede actuar
  como un vínculo cognitivo entre el duelo y la psicopatología. Por ejemplo, comparar con
   frecuencia el bienestar actual con los niveles previos a la pérdida (es decir, una comparación
   temporal con  el pasado) y  percibir una  diferencia  entre ambos  (discrepancia en  la
   comparación)  puede  intensificar  las  emociones  negativas  (impacto  afectivo  de  la
   comparación), lo que, a su vez, puede agravar la psicopatología. Planteamos la hipótesis de
  que  la  frecuencia de  comparaciones  aversivas de  bienestar,  la  discrepancia en  la
   comparación y el impacto afectivo negativo de la comparación predecirían, cada uno por
   separado, niveles más altos de psicopatología a lo largo del tiempo. Asimismo, se esperaba
  que  la discrepancia en la comparación y el impacto afectivo actuaran secuencialmente
  como mediadores de la relación entre la frecuencia de las comparaciones y la psicopatología.
  Método: Nuestro estudio longitudinal de dos olas con personas en duelo (N = 315) evaluó las
   comparaciones de bienestar, la preocupación, la rumiación, la evitación, las experiencias
   adversas en la infancia y los resultados de salud mental durante los seis meses posteriores a
    la pérdida.
   Resultados: Las hipótesis preregistradas se confirmaron parcialmente. Una mayor frecuencia
   de comparaciones aversivas de bienestar, la discrepancia en la comparación y el impacto

candidate: This longitudinal study investigated whether aversive well-being comparisons—including social, temporal, and counterfactual comparisons—serve as a cognitive link between bereavement and psychopathology. Using a two-wave design, researchers assessed 315 bereaved individuals at baseline and six months later. Participants were evaluated on comparison frequency, perceived discrepancy, and affective impact, alongside measures of prolonged grief disorder, PTSD, depression, anxiety, somatic symptoms, and loneliness. Results indicated that while grief and distress symptoms significantly decreased over six months, comparison frequency significantly predicted anxiety, somatic symptoms, and loneliness at the second assessment. Cross-sectional analyses revealed that comparison frequency significantly predicted depression, anxiety, and somatic symptoms, with these relationships mediated by perceived discrepancy and negative affective impact. Specifically, the indirect effects for depression (0.13, $p = .036$), anxiety (0.16, $p = .030$), and somatic symptoms (0.54, $p = .036$) were significant. The study concludes that aversive comparisons are independent predictors of distress, potentially exacerbating loss-oriented grieving. However, the study was limited by a 28% dropout rate, reliance on self-reports, and being underpowered to detect longitudinal mediation effects.

  pérdida: un estudio longitudinal de dos olas

   Antecedentes: La pérdida de un ser querido puede dar lugar al trastorno de duelo prolongado
   (TDP), al trastorno de estrés postraumático (TEPT), así como a depresión, ansiedad, síntomas
   somáticos y soledad. El pensamiento comparativo sobre el propio bienestar (por ejemplo,
   comparaciones sociales, temporales, contrafácticas o basadas en expectativas) puede actuar
  como un vínculo cognitivo entre el duelo y la psicopatología. Por ejemplo, comparar con
   frecuencia el bienestar actual con los niveles previos a la pérdida (es decir, una comparación
   temporal con  el pasado) y  percibir una  diferencia  entre ambos  (discrepancia en  la
   comparación)  puede  intensificar  las  emociones  negativas  (impacto  afectivo  de  la
   comparación), lo que, a su vez, puede agravar la psicopatología. Planteamos la hipótesis de
  que  la  frecuencia de  comparaciones  aversivas de  bienestar,  la  discrepancia en  la
   comparación y el impacto afectivo negativo de la comparación predecirían, cada uno por
   separado, niveles más altos de psicopatología a lo largo del tiempo. Asimismo, se esperaba
  que  la discrepancia en la comparación y el impacto afectivo actuaran secuencialmente
  como mediadores de la relación entre la frecuencia de las comparaciones y la psicopatología.
  Método: Nuestro estudio longitudinal de dos olas con personas en duelo (N = 315) evaluó las
   comparaciones de bienestar, la preocupación, la rumiación, la evitación, las experiencias
   adversas en la infancia y los resultados de salud mental durante los seis meses posteriores a
    la pérdida.
   Resultados: Las hipótesis preregistradas se confirmaron parcialmente. Una mayor frecuencia
   de comparaciones aversivas de bienestar, la discrepancia en la comparación y el impacto
   afectivo  negativo de  la  comparación  predijeron  niveles más  elevados de  síntomas
   psicopatológicos (TDP, TEPT, depresión, ansiedad, síntomas somáticos y soledad) seis meses
   después. Se observaron efectos matizados que se mantuvieron incluso al considerar las

candidate: This cross-sectional study investigated latent classes of adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) and their associations with impulsivity and mental health among adults in Saudi Arabia. Using an online convenience sample of 379 adults aged 18–65, researchers employed latent class analysis (LCA) to identify patterns of adversity. Participants were categorized into a structural no-ACE reference group and two ACE-exposed classes: limited/mixed ACE and poly-victimisation. The poly-victimisation class, characterized by high probabilities of emotional abuse, physical abuse, and household mental illness, showed significantly higher levels of negative urgency (d = 0.55) and lack of perseverance (d = 0.43) compared to the no-ACE group. Furthermore, this class was associated with a higher prevalence of lifetime psychiatric diagnosis (OR = 6.27) and greater perceived health impact (OR = 12.81). The study concludes that a poly-victimisation pattern is associated with greater emotion-related impulsivity and mental health burden, supporting the use of pattern-level assessments alongside cumulative ACE counts. Key limitations include the cross-sectional design, which precludes causal inference, the use of self-reported data, and the reliance on a convenience sample and brief, single-item mental health measures.

   Antecedentes: Las experiencias adversas en la infancia (ACEs por sus siglas en inglés) se
   asocian con problemas de salud mental en etapas posteriores, pero los recuentos simples
   de ACEs pueden ocultar qué adversidades coocurren en cada individuo. El modelamiento
   centrado en la persona puede identificar grupos de personas con patrones similares de
   exposición.
   Objetivo: Este estudio de corte transversal identificó clases latentes de ACEs entre adultos
   residentes en Arabia Saudita y examinó sus asociaciones con cinco facetas de la conducta
   impulsiva UPPS-P y con indicadores breves de salud mental.
   Método: Una muestra por conveniencia en línea de 379 adultos de entre 18 y 65 años
   completó el cuestionario de cribado de 10 ítems sobre ACEs, la versión árabe abreviada de
    la Escala UPPS-P de Conducta Impulsiva, y medidas de un solo ítem sobre el diagnóstico
   psiquiátrico de por vida y  el impacto percibido en  la salud. Los encuestados que no
   reportaron ACEs se mantuvieron como grupo de referencia estructural sin ACE, y el análisis
   de clases latentes se realizó entre los participantes expuestos a ACEs. La selección del
  modelo consideró criterios de información, entropía, probabilidades posteriores promedio,
  tamaño de clase e interpretabilidad. Las especificaciones alternativas de clases se evaluaron
   mediante  análisis  de  sensibilidad.  Se  aplicó  una  corrección  por  tasa  de  falsos
   descubrimientos (FDR, por sus siglas en inglés) a las pruebas pareadas de los resultados.

    las emociones y con una mayor carga en la salud mental. Los hallazgos respaldan el uso
   cauteloso de la evaluación de los ACEs a nivel de patrones, junto con los recuentos de ACEs,

candidate: This study investigated latent classes of adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) and their associations with impulsivity and mental health among adults in Saudi Arabia. A cross-sectional online survey of 379 adults aged 18–65 years was conducted, using the 10-item ACE screener, the Arabic Short UPPS-P Impulsive Behaviour Scale, and single-item measures of lifetime psychiatric diagnosis and perceived health impact. A structural no-ACE reference group was retained, and latent class analysis (LCA) identified two classes among ACE-exposed participants: limited/mixed ACE (n = 140, 36.9%) and poly-victimisation (n = 106, 28.0%). The poly-victimisation class showed higher negative urgency (d = 0.55, q < .001), lack of perseverance (d = 0.43, q = .007), psychiatric diagnosis (OR = 6.27, 95% CI [3.19, 12.31]), and perceived health impact (OR = 12.81, 95% CI [6.91, 23.75]) compared to the no-ACE group. Family conflict interactions were exploratory and not statistically robust. The findings suggest that poly-victimisation is associated with greater emotion-related impulsivity and mental health burden. While LCA provides complementary pattern-level information, it should not replace cumulative ACE scores. Limitations include the cross-sectional design, brief outcome measures, and potential biases in self-reporting. The study highlights the importance of considering ACE patterns in clinical and public health contexts.

  OR = 12,81; IC 95% [6,91, 23,75]). Las interacciones relacionadas con conflicto familiar fueron
   exploratorias y no estadísticamente robustas.
   Conclusión: Una clase de polivictimización se asoció con mayor impulsividad relacionada con
    las emociones y con una mayor carga en la salud mental. Los hallazgos respaldan el uso
   cauteloso de la evaluación de los ACEs a nivel de patrones, junto con los recuentos de ACEs,
   reconociendo  al mismo tiempo  las limitaciones del muestreo de corte transversal por
   conveniencia y de las medidas de resultados breves.

candidate: This study evaluated a national, three-tiered knowledge mobilization initiative designed to improve support for UK women veterans who have experienced military sexual trauma (MST). Guided by the Knowledge-to-Action framework and co-produced with women veterans, the program aimed to enhance professional knowledge, improve service engagement strategies, and increase clinical capacity for Cognitive Processing Therapy (CPT). The methodology employed a mixed-methods approach involving three components: a self-guided online foundational course for 526 individuals, a live online workshop for 363 professionals, and a truncated CPT training for 98 clinicians across 34 organizations. Quantitative analysis of the third course showed that clinician self-efficacy in delivering CPT significantly increased at a three-month follow-up ($p < .001, r = 0.915$), with a mean confidence increase of 1.00 (SE = 0.12). Qualitative findings highlighted themes regarding clinician confidence and systemic barriers to CPT delivery. The study concluded that the program successfully addressed knowledge gaps and demonstrated that co-produced knowledge mobilization can translate research into real-world impact. Limitations included low participation from Scotland, a potentially insufficient three-month follow-up period for assessing long-term systemic change, and the use of true-or-false quizzes for knowledge consolidation.

candidate: This paper describes a three-part online education and training program designed to enhance professional knowledge and improve support for UK women veterans who have experienced military sexual trauma (MST). Guided by knowledge mobilization (KMb) theory and the Knowledge-to-Action (KTA) framework, the program aimed to address gaps in service provider understanding and increase clinical capacity for evidence-based treatments, particularly cognitive processing therapy (CPT). The study involved 684 participants, including healthcare professionals, veteran specialists, and policy makers, who engaged with three courses: an introductory course on women veterans’ experiences, an advanced course on service adaptations, and a CPT training course. Mixed-methods data were collected, with quantitative analysis showing a significant increase in self-efficacy in delivering CPT among participants three months post-training (p < .001, r = 0.915). Qualitative feedback highlighted clinicians’ confidence in CPT, perceptions of its suitability for different patient groups, and challenges in implementation due to resource limitations and lack of training. The study found that the program successfully enhanced professional knowledge and supported the development of evidence-based practices, though limitations include the need for ongoing monitoring of long-term impact and broader engagement beyond veteran-specific organizations. The initiative demonstrates how research can be translated into real-world impact for military populations, emphasizing the value of co-produced KMb approaches.

candidate: This study is a population-based legacy analysis of myasthenia gravis (MG) in Iceland, aiming to assess its prevalence and incidence alongside clinical characteristics. Data were collected from 1981 to 2002 using hospital records, neurologists, immunology labs, and the national MG association, with inclusion requiring characteristic symptoms and at least one confirmatory test. Point prevalence was calculated on 31 December 2002, and incidence for 1997–2002. The study found a prevalence of 9.0 per 100,000 and a mean annual incidence of 0.78 per 100,000. The female-to-male ratio was 1.2:1, with a mean age at onset of 43 years. Ocular symptoms were predominant at presentation, and 19% experienced diagnostic delays exceeding three years. By 2003, 54% had generalized MG, and 27% were in complete remission. The study highlights the value of legacy datasets for rare disease surveillance, though it does not establish causality. Limitations include the small cohort size and potential underdiagnosis due to historical diagnostic practices. The findings align with global trends of increasing prevalence and incidence, suggesting improved detection and survival rates.

Introduction

Myasthenia gravis (MG) is an autoimmune neuromuscular disorder, classified among rare diseases by the
European Medicines Agency (EMA) as affecting fewer than 1 in 2000 individuals  [1]. Like many rare
conditions, MG is understudied due to low case numbers, geographic variability and the inherent difficulties
in gathering robust epidemiological data. These limitations hinder the development of a comprehensive
understanding of the disease's epidemiology, natural history and treatment responsiveness [2]. In this
context, every available data set, whether newly collected or historical, holds significant value. Increasing
attention  is being awarded to underutilized sources such as legacy cohorts, which allow temporal
comparisons, serve as benchmarks for trends in incidence and prevalence, and offer critical insight into
evolving diagnostic practices and disease trajectories over time [3,4].
  MG  is a well-recognized and  clinically complex neuromuscular disorder, characterized by fluctuating
weakness in voluntary muscles. Symptoms typically worsen with physical exertion and improve with rest,
often presenting as minimal in the morning and progressively intensifying throughout the day [5]. While the
exact cause remains unknown, it is well-established that a sizable proportion of patients produce autoantibodies
targeting acetylcholine receptors, leading to impaired neuromuscular transmission [6]. These immunological
changes are closely linked to thymic pathology, including thymomas in approximately 10–12% of patients [7]

and follicular hyperplasia in up to 70% [8]. These foundational findings continue to shape diagnostic criteria and
guide therapeutic approaches.
  The most common initial symptoms involve ocular muscles resulting in ptosis and/or diplopia, but the
disease may also affect bulbar, limb and trunk muscles. In severe cases, respiratory compromise may result
from involvement of the diaphragm and intercostal musculature [9]. MG can present at any age but is rare
before age 15 or after 70 [10]. Women are more commonly affected between the ages of 20–30, while men
are typically diagnosed later, between ages 50–70, with an overall male-to-female ratio of approximately 1:2
[11]. Treatment  is based on three primary  pillars: acetylcholinesterase inhibitors, immunosuppressive
therapy and thymectomy [9].
  Over the last two decades, the prevalence and incidence of MG have continued to rise globally, driven by
improved recognition, diagnostic tools and demographic shifts such as population aging [10,12,13]. To
shed light on these historical data, baselines are needed. Iceland's centralized healthcare system and
comprehensive  medical  record-keeping  provide  strength and  reliability  to  legacy  cohort  studies.
Importantly, analyzing data from earlier diagnostic sheds light on how diagnostic delays, treatment access
and remission patterns have evolved, especially prior to the widespread use of newer antibody tests (e.g.
anti-MuSK, anti-LRP4). Such insights are particularly valuable in rare disease contexts, where national
registries and longitudinal cohorts are pivotal for disease surveillance, resource allocation and shaping
policy [14,15].
  Over recent decades global epidemiological studies have demonstrated wide variations in MG preva­
lence and incidence across countries, attributed to greater awareness, improved diagnostics and population
aging [16]. Iceland, despite  its small population, has contributed meaningfully to this  field. The  first
population-based MG study, conducted in Iceland [17] was a landmark effort at a time when systematic
data on MG were limited. This early investigation reported a prevalence of 6.4 per 100,000 and an incidence
of 0.41 per 100,000. A follow-up, unpublished study in 1991 showed a slight increase in prevalence to 6.8
per 100,000, suggesting epidemiological stability across nearly three decades [18]. The present study aimed
to build upon this foundational work by providing a newer timepoint for the assessment of MG prevalence
and incidence in Iceland, alongside an in-depth characterization of  clinical presentation, diagnostic
practices, disease course and treatment patterns. The data, originally collected two decades ago, are
published here for the first time. Although not a longitudinal follow-up of previous cohorts, this analysis
serves as a legacy dataset, capturing a distinct historical period in MG care and diagnosis in Iceland, and
thereby enables valuable comparison with both earlier and future studies.


Methods

Design

This historical data aimed to establish the point prevalence and incidence of MG in Iceland during the
period (1997–2002), as well as to describe the clinical characteristics of the affected population. To ensure
comprehensive and transparent reporting, this study adhered to the STROBE (Strengthening the Reporting
of Observational Studies in Epidemiology) checklist [19].


Setting and participants
Patients with MG in Iceland were identified through electronic records from the Neurology Department of
Landspítali University Hospital using diagnostic codes ICD-9 358.0 and ICD-10 G70.0. The data search
covered the period from January 1, 1981, to December 31, 2002. Letters were sent to  all practicing
neurologists in Iceland and to the chief physicians of all primary healthcare centres across the country.
Records from the Immunology Laboratory at Landspítali, the only such laboratory in Iceland, were reviewed
for positive antibody test results from 1984 to 2002. The Icelandic MG patient association was informed
about the study, and members encouraged to contact the research team.
   After receiving permission from each patient's treating physician, an information letter and consent form
were sent to eligible patients. Subsequently, patients were invited to attend a clinical interview and
standardized examination at the Landspítali outpatient clinic. Those who were unable to attend provided
information about their medical history via telephone, and the most recent clinical assessment from their

INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF CIRCUMPOLAR HEALTH       3


physician was reviewed. This evaluation of the study cohort was conducted in February 2003. Population
data were obtained from Statistics Iceland.
   Inclusion in the study cohort required that the diagnosis be supported by at least one of the three
diagnostic criteria mentioned earlier: a positive response to acetylcholinesterase inhibitors, a decremental
muscle response to repetitive nerve stimulation, or a positive antibody test, in addition to characteristic
clinical symptoms. Congenital and drug-induced myasthenic syndromes were excluded.
   For clinical classification, the Osserman staging system was used [20]:


•  A = Asymptomatic without medication
•    I = Ocular symptoms only (diplopia/ptosis)
•   IIA = Mild generalized symptoms with minimal impact on daily life
•   IIB = Generalized symptoms causing significant functional impairment
•    III = Rapidly progressive generalized symptoms with prominent bulbar involvement
•  IV = Severe generalized symptoms with respiratory failure (myasthenic crisis)


   For comparability with contemporary epidemiological studies, Osserman classifications were retrospec­
tively mapped to the Myasthenia Gravis Foundation of America (MGFA) clinical classification [21] based on
documented symptom distribution and severity at assessment.


Data analysis

Descriptive statistics were used to summarize the demographic and clinical characteristics of the cohort.
Prevalence was calculated as point prevalence on 31 December 2002, when the population of Iceland was
288,471, and expressed per 100,000 inhabitants based on national census data. Incidence was calculated for
the five-year period from 31 December 1997, to 31 December 2002, and reported per 100,000 inhabitants
per year. Age at diagnosis and symptom onset were described using medians, interquartile ranges (IQR) and
full ranges. To explore associations between categorical variables (e.g. MG subtype and gender, or MG
subtype and treatment pattern), Fisher's exact test was used. Associations between continuous variables
and MG subtype (e.g. age at diagnosis) were assessed using the Mann–Whitney U test. The distribution of
age at diagnosis by MG type was visualized using a Seaborn violin plot, which integrates a kernel density
estimate with a boxplot to display both the overall data distribution and key summary statistics, including
the median and interquartile range. Statistical analyzes were conducted using SPSS, a p-value < 0.05 was
considered statistically significant.


Ethical considerations

The National Bioethics Committee (VSN-a2002110045) and the Icelandic Data Protection Authority (S1115/
2003) approved the study.


Results

Study population

Responses were received from all neurologists in Iceland and from 49 of 59 (83%) general practitioners
before the study period ended. Including the data from Landspítali University Hospital, a total of 57 patients
were initially identified. After further evaluation, 31 individuals were excluded, resulting in a final cohort of
26 patients. Of these, 21 patients attended clinical examinations and interviews.


Prevalence

The point prevalence of MG in Iceland as of 31 December 2002, was 26 out of 288,471 inhabitants alive that
day, equating to 9.0 per 100,000. The sex-specific prevalence was 9.7 per 100,000 for women and 8.3 for
men, with a male-to-female ratio of 1:1.2 (see Table 1).

Incidence

During the five-year period from 31 December 1997, to 31 December 2002, a total of 11 patients were
diagnosed with MG, corresponding to an annual incidence rate of 0.78 per 100,000 inhabitants.


Temporal gap between symptom onset and diagnosis

The median diagnostic delay was approximately 8 months. Eleven patients (42%) were diagnosed within six
months of symptom onset, and 18 (69%) within one year. In five patients (19%), the delay exceeded three
years, with the longest delay being 10 years. The mean age at symptom onset was 43 years (range: 5–84,
median: 42); for men, 59 years (range: 24–79, median: 60) and for women, 29 years (range: 5–84, median:
20). Symptoms began before the age of 45 in 12 of 14 women (86%) and after the age of 50 in 10 of 12 men
(83%) (see Figure 1).


Diagnosis confirmation

In 22 patients the clinical diagnosis was supported by positive antibody testing with acetylcholine receptor
antibodies (AChRAb). Eighteen had a positive response to acetylcholinesterase inhibitor testing (Tensilon),
and 15 had characteristic findings on electrophysiological studies. Figure 2 illustrates the overlap between
diagnostic modalities confirming the diagnosis. Numbers indicate patients with positive results in each

the largest number of cases, including patients not detected by Tensilon testing or neurophysiological
testing alone. Testing for muscle-specific kinase (MuSK) antibodies was not available in Iceland during the
study period.


Age at diagnosis

The mean age at diagnosis for all patients was 58 years (range: 13–89 years, median: 61 years); for men, the
mean was 70 years (range: 44–86 years, median: 73 years) and for women, 48 years (range: 13–89 years,
median: 47 years). Two patients were younger than 15 years at the time of diagnosis.
  The median age at diagnosis in the generalized MG group was 47.5 years (IQR: 27.5–60.8; range: 13–73),
compared to 55.0 years (IQR: 45.5–64.5; range: 24–89) in the ocular MG group. While there was a trend
toward younger age among patients with generalized MG, the interquartile ranges overlapped and a
Mann–Whitney U test indicated no significant difference in the distribution of ages at diagnosis between
groups (U = 38.0, p = 0.22). Figure 3 presents a combined violin and boxplot showing age at diagnosis by
MG type.


Disease course

In 19 patients (73%), ocular symptoms were part of the initial disease presentation. Among 15 patients
(58%) who initially only had ocular symptoms, 7 later developed generalized MG. Thirteen patients (50%)
had experienced exacerbations with generalized symptoms at some point during their illness, including
one case that needed mechanical ventilation. In total, 22 patients (85%) had been hospitalized due to MG,
with 15 (58%) requiring hospitalization more than once. Table 2 shows the classification of patients as
assessed in February 2003. Seven patients (27%) were asymptomatic and not receiving any treatment. In
five patients (19%)—all men—symptoms were confined to the eyes. Fourteen patients (54%) had general­
ized symptoms; in five of these cases (19%), the symptoms were severe enough to interfere with work
capacity and daily functioning.


Treatment in 2003

Twelve patients (46%) were not receiving any pharmacological therapy at the time of data collection.
Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors were used regularly by 11 patients (42%); among them, 5 (19%) relied on
this treatment alone, 4 (17%) combined  it with azathioprine and 2 (8%) received regular intravenous
immunoglobulin (IVIG) in addition. Based on contemporary definitions of refractory MG (persistent symp­
toms despite adequate immunosuppressive therapy or need for repeated rescue therapy), two patients
(8%) required regular IVIG despite immunosuppressive therapy and could retrospectively be classified as
having treatment-refractory MG according to contemporary definitions.

using the Osserman system, MGFA categories represent an approximate crosswalk rather than a formal MGFA assessment, intended to facilitate
comparison with contemporary literature.



   Three patients (12%) were treated exclusively with corticosteroids. Overall, 18 patients (69%) had
received immunosuppressive therapy at some point during the disease course, with corticosteroids
being the most frequently used agent (15 patients; 58%).
   Plasmapheresis was administered to 3 patients (12%) in response to severe disease exacerbation,
including one who underwent repeated procedures. Thymectomy had been performed in 11 patients
(42%). Histopathological examination of thymic tissue revealed lymphoid hyperplasia in 3 of the 11 cases
(27%) and thymic tumour in one case (9%). Of the 12 patients not receiving pharmacological treatment
(46%), 7 (27%) were asymptomatic and fulfilled criteria for complete remission. The remaining 5 patients
had mild persistent symptoms, primarily ocular, but did not require ongoing pharmacological therapy at
the time of evaluation.

INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF CIRCUMPOLAR HEALTH       7


Discussion

This population-based study provides comprehensive information on the epidemiology of MG in Iceland.
Although unpublished until now, the data retain scientific value adding to knowledge of MG in the Arctic
Circle and serves as a benchmark for future longitudinal analyzes. In rare disease research, particularly
within small, genetically homogeneous populations, legacy datasets are important for tracking epidemio­
logical trends and informing health system planning. Over the past two decades, MG prevalence has more
than doubled in many regions, driven by improved diagnostics and demographic shifts [13,22]. The
observed prevalence of MG in Iceland (9.0 per 100,000) represents a notable increase from earlier national
estimates: 6.4 per 100,000 in 1963 [17] and 6.8 per 100,000 in 1991 [18]. This upward trend likely reflects a
combination of improved survival, attributable to advances in treatment, as seen in other Nordic countries
[23,24], alongside increased case detection. These speculations are supported by the rise in incidence from
0.41 per 100,000/year during 1954–1963 to our findings 0.78 per 100,000/year during 1997–2002 [17,18].
Importantly, antibody testing was not available during the earliest Icelandic epidemiological study in 1963.
The introduction of acetylcholine receptor antibody assays in Iceland around the mid-1980s likely improved
diagnostic sensitivity and case ascertainment, particularly among patients with milder or atypical presen­
tations. This development may have contributed to the observed increase in both prevalence and incidence
over time. Earlier case identification relied primarily on clinical examination and pharmacological testing,
which may have led to underdiagnosis.
  Demographic changes, particularly an aging population, may play a role, as late-onset MG has become more
prevalent [22]. Since men are more frequently affected at older ages [10,25], this may partly explain the higher
proportion of men in our cohort (male-to-female ratio: 1:1.2), which contrasts with previous Icelandic and
international studies reporting ratios closer to 1:2 or 1:3 [26,27]. Overall, the prevalence figure in our study is
consistent with those reported in many international studies (see Table 3) [11,23,24,26,28–32].
  As shown in Table 3, three studies report notably higher MG prevalence rates (14–15 per 100,000). The
elevated prevalence observed in the Virginia study may partly reflect the inclusion of a higher proportion of
black individuals, among whom MG is thought to occur more frequently [31]. In the Cambridgeshire study,
less stringent diagnostic  criteria were applied compared to other studies, including our own,  likely
contributing to the higher figures [26]. In Stockholm, the existence of a specialized MG centre with
dedicated personnel likely improved both diagnostic rates and patient follow-up [11]. However, the
presence of such a referral centre may also have introduced bias, as patients from other parts of the
country could have relocated to Stockholm for specialized care, potentially inflating the reported regional
prevalence. This issue was not specifically addressed in the Swedish study. Nevertheless, the high preva­
lence reported raises the possibility that our own study may not have captured all diagnosed MG cases in
Iceland.
  Our results can also be compared with a recent systematic review and meta-analysis which estimated the
global prevalence of MG to be 12.4 per 100,000 (95% CI: 10.6–14.5), with slightly lower figures reported in
continental Europe (approximately 10 per 100,000) [33]. Other contemporary studies report rising rates of
MG worldwide  [34,35]. The precise drivers of these increased trends, whether improved diagnostic
sensitivity, heightened clinical awareness, or demographic shifts, remain an area of active and future

investigations. In this context, our study offers a meaningful historical base comparing a rare disease in a
small Arctic area which aligns with broader global trends.
   Patients presenting with clear ocular or bulbar symptoms were generally diagnosed without significant
delay. In contrast, patients with more nonspecific limb or facial symptoms experienced longer diagnostic
delays. Notably, one patient was misattributed with “chronic fatigue” for five years before the emergence of
ocular signs prompted reevaluation, while another was treated for anxiety for three years prior to the
eventual diagnosis of MG.
  Although 13 patients experienced disease exacerbations during the course of  illness, the overall
prognosis in this cohort was relatively favourable. At the time of data collection, 46% of patients were
either asymptomatic or had symptoms mild enough to require no ongoing medication, a notably higher
proportion than reported in the Swedish (12%) [11,35] and British (16%) cohorts [26]. This comparatively
positive outcome may reflect early recognition of typical ocular symptoms, effective long-term disease
management and the availability of specialist care within Iceland's centralized healthcare system. Overall,
treatment strategies in Iceland were broadly aligned with international standards, although steroid therapy
appeared to be used somewhat more frequently. The proportion of patients undergoing thymectomy
(42%) was comparable to figures reported elsewhere, including 57% in Sweden and 35% in the United
Kingdom [11,26], suggesting that local clinical practice was consistent with contemporaneous European
trends.
  The high proportion of patients requiring hospitalization (85%) may appear discordant with the generally
favourable long-term outcomes observed. However, during the study period, hospital admission was frequently
required for diagnostic confirmation (e.g. edrophonium testing), initiation of immunosuppressive therapy, and
monitoring during exacerbations. In a small healthcare system with centralized specialist services, inpatient
evaluation was often standard practice rather than an indicator of severe disease.
   At the time of the study, edrophonium (Tensilon) testing remained in clinical use in Iceland. Although
this pharmacologic challenge test has since been discontinued due to the risk of rare but serious adverse
effects, no such complications were observed in this cohort, and  its diagnostic  utility was evident,
contributing to confirmation in 18 patients. Since then, diagnostic practices have evolved substantially.
Advances in neurophysiological methods, including broader access to single-fibre electromyography (EMG)
and standardized training in repetitive nerve stimulation, have markedly improved the accuracy and
reliability of MG diagnosis in Iceland.


Strengths and limitations

Historical epidemiological data are often prone to bias due to population heterogeneity and geographic
variation [36]. The small cohort in our study limits the strength of the data but at the same time Iceland
offers an unusually robust context for such research, with a genetically and socially homogeneous
population and comprehensive national health records. This infrastructure allows for near-complete case
ascertainment across both primary and specialist care. Although the response rate from general practition­
ers was limited, some using ICD-code searches, others relying on recall,  all reported cases were also
documented in medical records and confirmed by neurologists. This high concordance, combined with
direct contact with all identified MG patients through in-person or telephone interviews, strengthens the
reliability of the data and the validity of the prevalence estimates. Additionally, MGFA classification was
retrospectively approximated from Osserman staging, which may introduce minor misclassification com­
pared with contemporaneous MGFA assessment.


Conclusion

This study provides valuable epidemiological and clinical insights into MG within the Icelandic population
and contributes to the enduring importance of historical datasets in rare disease research. Such data plays a
role in strengthening national surveillance systems, enabling longitudinal comparisons and informing
global understanding of disease patterns, considering small and geographically distinct populations such
as those in the Arctic region.

Inclusion required characteristic symptoms and at least one confirmatory test, such as positive acetylcholine receptor antibodies (AChRAb), positive response to acetylcholinesterase inhibitors, or abnormal electrophysiology. Introduction

Myasthenia gravis (MG) is an autoimmune neuromuscular disorder, classified among rare diseases by the
European Medicines Agency (EMA) as affecting fewer than 1 in 2000 individuals  [1]. Like many rare
conditions, MG is understudied due to low case numbers, geographic variability and the inherent difficulties
in gathering robust epidemiological data. These limitations hinder the development of a comprehensive
understanding of the disease's epidemiology, natural history and treatment responsiveness [2]. In this
context, every available data set, whether newly collected or historical, holds significant value. Increasing
attention  is being awarded to underutilized sources such as legacy cohorts, which allow temporal
comparisons, serve as benchmarks for trends in incidence and prevalence, and offer critical insight into
evolving diagnostic practices and disease trajectories over time [3,4].
  MG  is a well-recognized and  clinically complex neuromuscular disorder, characterized by fluctuating
weakness in voluntary muscles. Symptoms typically worsen with physical exertion and improve with rest,
often presenting as minimal in the morning and progressively intensifying throughout the day [5]. While the
exact cause remains unknown, it is well-established that a sizable proportion of patients produce autoantibodies
targeting acetylcholine receptors, leading to impaired neuromuscular transmission [6]. These immunological
changes are closely linked to thymic pathology, including thymomas in approximately 10–12% of patients [7]

and follicular hyperplasia in up to 70% [8]. These foundational findings continue to shape diagnostic criteria and
guide therapeutic approaches.
  The most common initial symptoms involve ocular muscles resulting in ptosis and/or diplopia, but the
disease may also affect bulbar, limb and trunk muscles. In severe cases, respiratory compromise may result
from involvement of the diaphragm and intercostal musculature [9]. MG can present at any age but is rare
before age 15 or after 70 [10]. Women are more commonly affected between the ages of 20–30, while men
are typically diagnosed later, between ages 50–70, with an overall male-to-female ratio of approximately 1:2
[11]. Treatment  is based on three primary  pillars: acetylcholinesterase inhibitors, immunosuppressive
therapy and thymectomy [9].
  Over the last two decades, the prevalence and incidence of MG have continued to rise globally, driven by
improved recognition, diagnostic tools and demographic shifts such as population aging [10,12,13]. To
shed light on these historical data, baselines are needed. Iceland's centralized healthcare system and
comprehensive  medical  record-keeping  provide  strength and  reliability  to  legacy  cohort  studies.
Importantly, analyzing data from earlier diagnostic sheds light on how diagnostic delays, treatment access
and remission patterns have evolved, especially prior to the widespread use of newer antibody tests (e.g.
anti-MuSK, anti-LRP4). Such insights are particularly valuable in rare disease contexts, where national
registries and longitudinal cohorts are pivotal for disease surveillance, resource allocation and shaping
policy [14,15].
  Over recent decades global epidemiological studies have demonstrated wide variations in MG preva­
lence and incidence across countries, attributed to greater awareness, improved diagnostics and population
aging [16]. Iceland, despite  its small population, has contributed meaningfully to this  field. The  first
population-based MG study, conducted in Iceland [17] was a landmark effort at a time when systematic
data on MG were limited. This early investigation reported a prevalence of 6.4 per 100,000 and an incidence
of 0.41 per 100,000. A follow-up, unpublished study in 1991 showed a slight increase in prevalence to 6.8
per 100,000, suggesting epidemiological stability across nearly three decades [18]. The present study aimed
to build upon this foundational work by providing a newer timepoint for the assessment of MG prevalence
and incidence in Iceland, alongside an in-depth characterization of  clinical presentation, diagnostic
practices, disease course and treatment patterns. The data, originally collected two decades ago, are
published here for the first time. Although not a longitudinal follow-up of previous cohorts, this analysis
serves as a legacy dataset, capturing a distinct historical period in MG care and diagnosis in Iceland, and
thereby enables valuable comparison with both earlier and future studies.


Methods

Design

This historical data aimed to establish the point prevalence and incidence of MG in Iceland during the
period (1997–2002), as well as to describe the clinical characteristics of the affected population. To ensure
comprehensive and transparent reporting, this study adhered to the STROBE (Strengthening the Reporting
of Observational Studies in Epidemiology) checklist [19].


Setting and participants
Patients with MG in Iceland were identified through electronic records from the Neurology Department of
Landspítali University Hospital using diagnostic codes ICD-9 358.0 and ICD-10 G70.0. The data search
covered the period from January 1, 1981, to December 31, 2002. Letters were sent to  all practicing
neurologists in Iceland and to the chief physicians of all primary healthcare centres across the country.
Records from the Immunology Laboratory at Landspítali, the only such laboratory in Iceland, were reviewed
for positive antibody test results from 1984 to 2002. The Icelandic MG patient association was informed
about the study, and members encouraged to contact the research team.
   After receiving permission from each patient's treating physician, an information letter and consent form
were sent to eligible patients. Subsequently, patients were invited to attend a clinical interview and
standardized examination at the Landspítali outpatient clinic. Those who were unable to attend provided
information about their medical history via telephone, and the most recent clinical assessment from their

INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF CIRCUMPOLAR HEALTH       3


physician was reviewed. This evaluation of the study cohort was conducted in February 2003. Population
data were obtained from Statistics Iceland.
   Inclusion in the study cohort required that the diagnosis be supported by at least one of the three
diagnostic criteria mentioned earlier: a positive response to acetylcholinesterase inhibitors, a decremental
muscle response to repetitive nerve stimulation, or a positive antibody test, in addition to characteristic
clinical symptoms. Congenital and drug-induced myasthenic syndromes were excluded.
   For clinical classification, the Osserman staging system was used [20]:


•  A = Asymptomatic without medication
•    I = Ocular symptoms only (diplopia/ptosis)
•   IIA = Mild generalized symptoms with minimal impact on daily life
•   IIB = Generalized symptoms causing significant functional impairment
•    III = Rapidly progressive generalized symptoms with prominent bulbar involvement
•  IV = Severe generalized symptoms with respiratory failure (myasthenic crisis)


   For comparability with contemporary epidemiological studies, Osserman classifications were retrospec­
tively mapped to the Myasthenia Gravis Foundation of America (MGFA) clinical classification [21] based on
documented symptom distribution and severity at assessment.


Data analysis

Descriptive statistics were used to summarize the demographic and clinical characteristics of the cohort.
Prevalence was calculated as point prevalence on 31 December 2002, when the population of Iceland was
288,471, and expressed per 100,000 inhabitants based on national census data. Incidence was calculated for
the five-year period from 31 December 1997, to 31 December 2002, and reported per 100,000 inhabitants
per year. Age at diagnosis and symptom onset were described using medians, interquartile ranges (IQR) and
full ranges. To explore associations between categorical variables (e.g. MG subtype and gender, or MG
subtype and treatment pattern), Fisher's exact test was used. Associations between continuous variables
and MG subtype (e.g. age at diagnosis) were assessed using the Mann–Whitney U test. The distribution of
age at diagnosis by MG type was visualized using a Seaborn violin plot, which integrates a kernel density
estimate with a boxplot to display both the overall data distribution and key summary statistics, including
the median and interquartile range. Statistical analyzes were conducted using SPSS, a p-value < 0.05 was
considered statistically significant.


Ethical considerations

The National Bioethics Committee (VSN-a2002110045) and the Icelandic Data Protection Authority (S1115/
2003) approved the study.


Results

Study population

Responses were received from all neurologists in Iceland and from 49 of 59 (83%) general practitioners
before the study period ended. Including the data from Landspítali University Hospital, a total of 57 patients
were initially identified. After further evaluation, 31 individuals were excluded, resulting in a final cohort of
26 patients. Of these, 21 patients attended clinical examinations and interviews.


Prevalence

The point prevalence of MG in Iceland as of 31 December 2002, was 26 out of 288,471 inhabitants alive that
day, equating to 9.0 per 100,000. The sex-specific prevalence was 9.7 per 100,000 for women and 8.3 for
men, with a male-to-female ratio of 1:1.2 (see Table 1).

Incidence

During the five-year period from 31 December 1997, to 31 December 2002, a total of 11 patients were
diagnosed with MG, corresponding to an annual incidence rate of 0.78 per 100,000 inhabitants.


Temporal gap between symptom onset and diagnosis

The median diagnostic delay was approximately 8 months. Eleven patients (42%) were diagnosed within six
months of symptom onset, and 18 (69%) within one year. In five patients (19%), the delay exceeded three
years, with the longest delay being 10 years. The mean age at symptom onset was 43 years (range: 5–84,
median: 42); for men, 59 years (range: 24–79, median: 60) and for women, 29 years (range: 5–84, median:
20). Symptoms began before the age of 45 in 12 of 14 women (86%) and after the age of 50 in 10 of 12 men
(83%) (see Figure 1).


Diagnosis confirmation

In 22 patients the clinical diagnosis was supported by positive antibody testing with acetylcholine receptor
antibodies (AChRAb). Eighteen had a positive response to acetylcholinesterase inhibitor testing (Tensilon),
and 15 had characteristic findings on electrophysiological studies. Figure 2 illustrates the overlap between
diagnostic modalities confirming the diagnosis. Numbers indicate patients with positive results in each

Age at diagnosis

The mean age at diagnosis for all patients was 58 years (range: 13–89 years, median: 61 years); for men, the
mean was 70 years (range: 44–86 years, median: 73 years) and for women, 48 years (range: 13–89 years,
median: 47 years). Two patients were younger than 15 years at the time of diagnosis.
  The median age at diagnosis in the generalized MG group was 47.5 years (IQR: 27.5–60.8; range: 13–73),
compared to 55.0 years (IQR: 45.5–64.5; range: 24–89) in the ocular MG group. While there was a trend
toward younger age among patients with generalized MG, the interquartile ranges overlapped and a
Mann–Whitney U test indicated no significant difference in the distribution of ages at diagnosis between
groups (U = 38.0, p = 0.22). Figure 3 presents a combined violin and boxplot showing age at diagnosis by
MG type.


Disease course

In 19 patients (73%), ocular symptoms were part of the initial disease presentation. Among 15 patients
(58%) who initially only had ocular symptoms, 7 later developed generalized MG. Thirteen patients (50%)
had experienced exacerbations with generalized symptoms at some point during their illness, including
one case that needed mechanical ventilation. In total, 22 patients (85%) had been hospitalized due to MG,
with 15 (58%) requiring hospitalization more than once. Table 2 shows the classification of patients as
assessed in February 2003. Seven patients (27%) were asymptomatic and not receiving any treatment. In
five patients (19%)—all men—symptoms were confined to the eyes. Fourteen patients (54%) had general­
ized symptoms; in five of these cases (19%), the symptoms were severe enough to interfere with work
capacity and daily functioning.


Treatment in 2003

Twelve patients (46%) were not receiving any pharmacological therapy at the time of data collection.
Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors were used regularly by 11 patients (42%); among them, 5 (19%) relied on
this treatment alone, 4 (17%) combined  it with azathioprine and 2 (8%) received regular intravenous
immunoglobulin (IVIG) in addition. Based on contemporary definitions of refractory MG (persistent symp­
toms despite adequate immunosuppressive therapy or need for repeated rescue therapy), two patients
(8%) required regular IVIG despite immunosuppressive therapy and could retrospectively be classified as
having treatment-refractory MG according to contemporary definitions.

Discussion

This population-based study provides comprehensive information on the epidemiology of MG in Iceland.
Although unpublished until now, the data retain scientific value adding to knowledge of MG in the Arctic
Circle and serves as a benchmark for future longitudinal analyzes. In rare disease research, particularly
within small, genetically homogeneous populations, legacy datasets are important for tracking epidemio­
logical trends and informing health system planning. Over the past two decades, MG prevalence has more
than doubled in many regions, driven by improved diagnostics and demographic shifts [13,22]. The
observed prevalence of MG in Iceland (9.0 per 100,000) represents a notable increase from earlier national
estimates: 6.4 per 100,000 in 1963 [17] and 6.8 per 100,000 in 1991 [18]. This upward trend likely reflects a
combination of improved survival, attributable to advances in treatment, as seen in other Nordic countries
[23,24], alongside increased case detection. These speculations are supported by the rise in incidence from
0.41 per 100,000/year during 1954–1963 to our findings 0.78 per 100,000/year during 1997–2002 [17,18].
Importantly, antibody testing was not available during the earliest Icelandic epidemiological study in 1963.
The introduction of acetylcholine receptor antibody assays in Iceland around the mid-1980s likely improved
diagnostic sensitivity and case ascertainment, particularly among patients with milder or atypical presen­
tations. This development may have contributed to the observed increase in both prevalence and incidence
over time. Earlier case identification relied primarily on clinical examination and pharmacological testing,
which may have led to underdiagnosis.
  Demographic changes, particularly an aging population, may play a role, as late-onset MG has become more
prevalent [22]. Since men are more frequently affected at older ages [10,25], this may partly explain the higher
proportion of men in our cohort (male-to-female ratio: 1:1.2), which contrasts with previous Icelandic and
international studies reporting ratios closer to 1:2 or 1:3 [26,27]. Overall, the prevalence figure in our study is
consistent with those reported in many international studies (see Table 3) [11,23,24,26,28–32].
  As shown in Table 3, three studies report notably higher MG prevalence rates (14–15 per 100,000). The
elevated prevalence observed in the Virginia study may partly reflect the inclusion of a higher proportion of
black individuals, among whom MG is thought to occur more frequently [31]. In the Cambridgeshire study,
less stringent diagnostic  criteria were applied compared to other studies, including our own,  likely
contributing to the higher figures [26]. In Stockholm, the existence of a specialized MG centre with
dedicated personnel likely improved both diagnostic rates and patient follow-up [11]. However, the
presence of such a referral centre may also have introduced bias, as patients from other parts of the
country could have relocated to Stockholm for specialized care, potentially inflating the reported regional
prevalence. This issue was not specifically addressed in the Swedish study. Nevertheless, the high preva­
lence reported raises the possibility that our own study may not have captured all diagnosed MG cases in
Iceland.
  Our results can also be compared with a recent systematic review and meta-analysis which estimated the
global prevalence of MG to be 12.4 per 100,000 (95% CI: 10.6–14.5), with slightly lower figures reported in
continental Europe (approximately 10 per 100,000) [33]. Other contemporary studies report rising rates of
MG worldwide  [34,35]. The precise drivers of these increased trends, whether improved diagnostic
sensitivity, heightened clinical awareness, or demographic shifts, remain an area of active and future

investigations. In this context, our study offers a meaningful historical base comparing a rare disease in a
small Arctic area which aligns with broader global trends.
   Patients presenting with clear ocular or bulbar symptoms were generally diagnosed without significant
delay. In contrast, patients with more nonspecific limb or facial symptoms experienced longer diagnostic
delays. Notably, one patient was misattributed with “chronic fatigue” for five years before the emergence of
ocular signs prompted reevaluation, while another was treated for anxiety for three years prior to the
eventual diagnosis of MG.
  Although 13 patients experienced disease exacerbations during the course of  illness, the overall
prognosis in this cohort was relatively favourable. At the time of data collection, 46% of patients were
either asymptomatic or had symptoms mild enough to require no ongoing medication, a notably higher
proportion than reported in the Swedish (12%) [11,35] and British (16%) cohorts [26]. This comparatively
positive outcome may reflect early recognition of typical ocular symptoms, effective long-term disease
management and the availability of specialist care within Iceland's centralized healthcare system. Overall,
treatment strategies in Iceland were broadly aligned with international standards, although steroid therapy
appeared to be used somewhat more frequently. The proportion of patients undergoing thymectomy
(42%) was comparable to figures reported elsewhere, including 57% in Sweden and 35% in the United
Kingdom [11,26], suggesting that local clinical practice was consistent with contemporaneous European
trends.
  The high proportion of patients requiring hospitalization (85%) may appear discordant with the generally
favourable long-term outcomes observed. However, during the study period, hospital admission was frequently
required for diagnostic confirmation (e.g. edrophonium testing), initiation of immunosuppressive therapy, and
monitoring during exacerbations. In a small healthcare system with centralized specialist services, inpatient
evaluation was often standard practice rather than an indicator of severe disease.
   At the time of the study, edrophonium (Tensilon) testing remained in clinical use in Iceland. Although
this pharmacologic challenge test has since been discontinued due to the risk of rare but serious adverse
effects, no such complications were observed in this cohort, and  its diagnostic  utility was evident,
contributing to confirmation in 18 patients. Since then, diagnostic practices have evolved substantially.
Advances in neurophysiological methods, including broader access to single-fibre electromyography (EMG)
and standardized training in repetitive nerve stimulation, have markedly improved the accuracy and
reliability of MG diagnosis in Iceland.


Strengths and limitations

Historical epidemiological data are often prone to bias due to population heterogeneity and geographic
variation [36]. The small cohort in our study limits the strength of the data but at the same time Iceland
offers an unusually robust context for such research, with a genetically and socially homogeneous
population and comprehensive national health records. This infrastructure allows for near-complete case
ascertainment across both primary and specialist care. Although the response rate from general practition­
ers was limited, some using ICD-code searches, others relying on recall,  all reported cases were also
documented in medical records and confirmed by neurologists. This high concordance, combined with
direct contact with all identified MG patients through in-person or telephone interviews, strengthens the
reliability of the data and the validity of the prevalence estimates. Additionally, MGFA classification was
retrospectively approximated from Osserman staging, which may introduce minor misclassification com­
pared with contemporaneous MGFA assessment.


Conclusion

This study provides valuable epidemiological and clinical insights into MG within the Icelandic population
and contributes to the enduring importance of historical datasets in rare disease research. Such data plays a
role in strengthening national surveillance systems, enabling longitudinal comparisons and informing
global understanding of disease patterns, considering small and geographically distinct populations such
as those in the Arctic region.

Participants were assigned to receive either the fiber mixture or an isocaloric maltodextrin placebo while adhering to a high-protein, partially plant-based diet. The primary outcome was peripheral insulin sensitivity (IS) measured via hyperinsulinemic-euglycemic clamp. Results indicated that the fiber group showed a trend toward lower peripheral insulin sensitivity compared to the placebo group (p=0.081), while whole-body IS significantly decreased in the fiber group (p=0.034).    assessed the effects of daily potato fiber/sugar beet pectin supplementation (fiber,
   n = 19) versus maltodextrin (placebo, n = 21), both added to a high-protein diet (25E%
   protein, ±45% plant-based), on peripheral insulin sensitivity (IS) in adults with over­
   weight/obesity. Secondary outcomes included tissue-specific  IS, body composition,
   microbial composition and functionality, substrate metabolism, and gut permeability.
   Peripheral IS tended to decrease after fiber supplementation compared to placebo
   (p = 0.081), while whole-body IS significantly decreased (p = 0.034). Fiber mitigated the
   increase in insulin-mediated carbohydrate oxidation (p = 0.027) and decrease in fat
   oxidation (p = 0.006) that occurred in the placebo group. Additionally, fiber prevented
   an increase in protein oxidation (p = 0.048), while increasing colonic gut permeability
   (p = 0.046) and plasma interleukin-6 (p = 0.025). Body composition, microbial composi­
    tion, and fecal and circulating metabolites remained unchanged. In conclusion, fibers
   combined with a high-protein diet reduced (peripheral) IS and decreased metabolic
    flexibility compared to placebo. Reduced protein oxidation after fiber may reflect
   diminished amino acid bioavailability. Additionally, coadministration of fiber and pro­
   tein may compromise gut barrier function and inflammatory responses. More research
   investigating the interplay between dietary fibers and proteins is needed.



Introduction

The rising prevalence of obesity and obesity-related diseases, including type 2 diabetes (T2D), poses an
increased burden on healthcare systems worldwide. Accumulating evidence suggests that the microbiome
may play a prominent role in these diseases,1-5 being responsible for the fermentation of undigested food
in the colon, including dietary fibers and proteins. Fermentation of dietary fibers produces short-chain
fatty acids (SCFA), which can positively affect cardiometabolic health, improving multiorgan insulin
resistance and reducing inflammation, among others.1-3,6-8 However, fibers become depleted towards the
distal colon, initiating proteolytic fermentation instead, which produces a wide range of microbial

metabolites, including branched-chain fatty acids (BCFA), ammonia, p-cresol, and hydrogen sulfide. These
metabolites are often associated with detrimental health effects, including reduced gut barrier function,
diminished lipid oxidative capacity, and increased inflammation.2
   Previous studies have shown that acute distal, but not proximal, colonic SCFA administration induces
increased lipid oxidation and reduced plasma inflammatory markers,3,6 suggesting that interventions
increasing distal saccharolytic fermentation, and potentially inhibiting proteolytic fermentation, may
alleviate cardiometabolic disturbances.1,9 However, not every fiber induces  distal SCFA production.
Fermentable fibers with a low molecular mass and a less complex structure (e.g., oligosaccharides) are
rapidly fermented in the proximal colon, whereas more complex fibers might be fermented slowly and
thereby reach the distal colon. Thus, combining dietary fibers with different fermentation rates may
promote saccharolytic fermentation distally, as was shown in a recent study, combining long-chain inulin
and resistant starch, which increased distal SCFA production in vitro,10 and provided acute metabolic
improvements in vivo in lean individuals.10 However, in vitro SCFA production by the microbiota of
individuals with obesity was not increased,10 and no effects on metabolic health were observed in vivo in
individuals with prediabetes. This might be explained by differences in the gut microbiome between
individuals with normal weight and obesity and prediabetes,2,11,12 evidenced by lower microbial diversity
and fewer SCFA-producing taxa in individuals with overweight, potentially with increased protein
degradation capacities.4,5,11 Hence, metabolic phenotype, initial microbiota composition, and the micro­
biota's SCFA-producing capacity may be important determinants of response to nutritional interven­
tions.4,11-13
   Besides differences in fiber type and metabolic phenotype, combining fibers and (plant-based) proteins
might influence the effects of fiber-induced steering of colonic fermentation and, subsequently, metabolic
processes. Since current nutritional guidelines generally aim to  shift toward plant-based diets and
increased dietary fiber intake, understanding fiber–protein interactions  is  essential.7,14 While plant-
based diets in general have been associated with cardiometabolic benefits,15 and plant-derived proteins
may improve insulin sensitivity, inflammatory processes, and body weight control,16-18 the impact of
indigestible plant-based proteins on microbial composition and functionality is still insufficiently under­
stood. Plant-based, compared to animal-based, proteins are generally  less  digestible,18,19 potentially
increasing proteolytic fermentation in the colon. Since proteolytic fermentation might already be increased
in individuals with obesity, understanding the microbial and metabolic effects of combining (plant-based)
proteins and dietary fibers in a long-term setting in a population at risk of developing T2D and
cardiometabolic complications is essential.
   In this randomized-controlled trial, we aimed to steer microbial fermentation processes in the human
colon through a potato fiber/sugar beet pectin supplement, known to stimulate distal colonic SCFA
production in vitro,20 within the context of a high-protein diet (±45% plant-based) in individuals at risk of
developing T2D. We intended to increase saccharolytic and inhibit proteolytic fermentation in the distal
colon, thereby improving metabolic health through altered microbial metabolite production, including
peripheral insulin sensitivity (IS) as the primary outcome. Secondary outcomes were hepatic and adipose
tissue, as well as whole-body IS, substrate oxidation, body composition, circulating cardiometabolic
markers, and microbial composition and functionality as secondary outcomes.


Methods

Recruitment and study registration

The DISTAL study was a 12-week, parallel, double-blind, placebo-controlled dietary intervention, investi­
gating the effects of potato fiber and sugar beet pectin supplementation versus an isocaloric placebo, both
within the context of a high-protein diet (25E% protein, ±45% plant-based), in 44 adults with overweight/
obesity and impaired glucose metabolism (30–75 y, BMI 28–40 kg/m2, exhibiting signs of insulin resist­
ance, based on either fasting glucose (5.6–6.9 mmol/l), HbA1c (42–47 mmol/mol), or HOMA-IR (>1.85))
(Figure 1). This single-center study was conducted between September 2022 and June 2024 at Maastricht
University  Medical  Center+ (MUMC+,  Maastricht,  the  Netherlands) and  Maastricht  University
(Maastricht  University,  Maastricht,  the  Netherlands), was approved by  the  local Medical  Ethics

Primary and secondary outcome measures

We assessed the effects of a potato fiber and sugar beet pectin mixture, within the context of a high-
protein, partially plant-based diet, versus placebo (maltodextrin) on peripheral insulin sensitivity (IS),
measured by the two-step hyperinsulinemic-euglycemic clamp as our primary outcome, and on tissue-
specific and whole-body IS, substrate and energy metabolism, cardiometabolic markers, microbial com­
position and functionality, gut permeability, and general well-being as secondary outcomes.


Potato fiber and sugar beet pectin supplementation

The investigated fiber mixture was based on our previous in vitro experiments, in which the current
combination yielded the most saccharolytic fermentation and SCFA production in the distal colon.20
Participants were randomized using minimization for age, sex, and BMI to either of the intervention

groups (the potato fiber and sugar beet pectin mixture (fiber) or an isocaloric placebo (maltodextrin)). The
fiber supplement consisted of 15 g/d (50:50 potato fiber:sugar beet pectin). Both fiber and placebo were
distributed in three equal-weight sachets per day, one for each meal. Participants were instructed to start
using the supplements and adhering to the high-protein diet the day after CID2 until the day before CID3,
and to return all provided sachets at the end of the intervention to assess adherence.


High-plant-protein dietary intervention

Both groups were instructed to adhere to a high-protein, partially plant-based diet. This diet consisted of
25 energy-% (E%) proteins, 30E% fats (<30% saturated fats), and 45E% carbohydrates, all in line with
Dutch dietary guidelines.21,22 The protein content was aimed at 45% plant-based, and fiber consumption at
approximately 30 g/d (fiber supplement not included). Our in-house dietician provided written and verbal
instructions of the diet, which was tailored to participants' energy requirements and personal preferences
to maintain weight stability and increase dietary adherence.


Study procedures

Extensive details on study design, the dietary intervention, participant characteristics, recruitment (includ­
ing a flow-chart (Supplementary figure 1)), and randomization, as well as detailed descriptions of the
conducted experiments and related analyzes, can be found in the Supplementary methods. A brief
description of the included experiments can be found below.


Tissue-specific insulin sensitivity
The two-step hyperinsulinemic-euglycemic clamp, the gold standard for measuring tissue-specific and
whole-body IS, was performed after a >10 h overnight fast on CID2 and CID4, which was preceded by
consumption of a standardized meal (See supplementary materials for more details). At first, a [6,6-2H2]
glucose tracer is infused for 2 h, after which low-dose insulin infusion (10 mU/m2/min) was added for
three hours to allow calculation of hepatic and adipose-tissue  IS. Afterwards, insulin infusion was
increased to 40 mU/m2/min to determine peripheral and whole-body IS (by means of the rate of glucose
appearance (Ra), glucose disposal (Rd), Rd per unit of circulating insulin (Rd/I), glucose infusion rates
(GIR), and M values). Insulin-mediated free fatty acid suppression was calculated at the end of the low step
as a measure of adipose tissue (AT) insulin sensitivity.


Energy expenditure and substrate metabolism
During the last thirty minutes of each step of the clamp, open-circuit indirect calorimetry was conducted
using a ventilated hood system to assess energy expenditure and substrate utilization, calculated by Weir
and Frayn equations.23,24 24 h urinary nitrogen excretion was incorporated to accurately determine protein
oxidation. Furthermore, metabolic flexibility was assessed by calculating the difference in respiratory
quotient between baseline and the high step and the switch in insulin-stimulated substrate oxidation.


Body composition, anthropometry, and blood pressure
 Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DEXA) was performed at CID1 and CID3 to determine body fat mass,
fat-free mass, fat distribution, and visceral adipose tissue. Body weight, waist and hip circumferences, and
blood pressure were measured on CID1, weeks 2 and 6, and CID3.


Cardiometabolic markers
Fasting blood samples were obtained at CID2 and CID4, and during the week-6 visit after an overnight fast
to assess cardiometabolic markers, including glucose, insulin, glycated hemoglobin A1 (HbA1c), free-fatty
acids (FFA), inflammatory markers (interleukin (IL)-6, IL-8, IL-10, tumor necrosis factor-α (TNA-α),
interferon-γ (IFN-γ), C-reactive protein (CRP), and leukocytes), lipid profile, lipopolysaccharide-binding
protein (LBP), satiety hormones (Peptide YY (PYY) and glucagon-like peptide 1 (GLP-1)), and SCFA
and BCFA.
